utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination will now continue. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor, how are you today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday we got as far as November 1998. Between March and November, as you said, you travelled a number of times to talk to members of the representatives of the Albanian community. There were talks with Chris Hill, O'Brien, proposals were made, counter-proposals were made concerning certain documents. Did a document come about as a result of all of that eventually?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a document was eventually produced by those involved in the talks, meaning the representatives of all ethnic minorities in Kosovo and Metohija including the Albanians, with the exception of their major political parties on the one hand and the state delegation on the other. The result of those talks was the agreement on self-management or self-administration in Kosovo and Metohija. It was by a joint effort that this policy was formulated. This began on the 12th of March, and then in November the final text was produced. Again, I must emphasise that the representatives of the majority Albanian parties took part in the talks and drafting of this document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Did not take part in the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can I please ask you to take one thing at a time. Could you please go to tab 42, 1D091. This is the joint proposal on the agreement on self-government in Kosovo and Metohija dated the 20th of November, 1998. Is that the agreement you told us about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the agreement. Can I just go through it, please. Yes, yes, this is the agreement. This is in actual fact a joint proposal formulated by those involved in this series of talks in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just very briefly please tell us about the crucial points of this agreement, the way you see the crucial points of this agreement as they relate to the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement establishes what according to its author should constitute the essence of self-government in Kosovo and Metohija. I will only comment on the principles, not about the operational measures. That can be read in the agreement itself. The substance of the agreement is that Kosovo and Metohija is a multi-ethnic community and that no single ethnic community, regardless of its size, may be allowed to demean or slight any other ethnic minorities. And that's why everyone should be consulted when dealing with issues of major national interest. This mechanism would be set in motion by a special method of decision-making in the Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija as its one major political body. Given the fact that Kosovo and Metohija as part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of the Republic of Serbia, is a mechanism of representation of the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija in the federal organs, in the republican organs, the functioning of the local police was determined as well as its organisation and a mechanism was envisaged for further amendments to the agreement. This would be it in a very rough outline but I must repeat that Kosovo and Metohija and that is key to this issue, is a multi-ethnic community where no ethnic community may be allowed to exercise any sort of domination or supremacy over other ethnic communities just because of its size.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this political agreement was signed by certain numbers of the representatives of Kosovo's ethnic minorities, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was signed by all the representatives of all the ethnic minorities that were actually involved in formulating this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about this agreement that was signed by all the ethnic minorities that were involved in the talks surrounding the agreement, was there access to this agreement by any other interested parties that may or may not have been around?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was open to anyone, and we would have been very glad for the representatives of the major Albanian parties to be involved in the talks, but as we said yesterday they refused to be involved in these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the agreement was signed by whoever was involved in the talks. Would the delegation of the Republic of Serbia not, nevertheless, have been prepared to consider amendments to the agreement had the representatives of the majority Albanian parties submitted anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started with a blank sheet of paper. There was nothing on it. Whoever was invited would have been allowed to have a say. The representatives of the majority Albanian political parties had been invited. It was self-implicit that they, too, would have been allowed a say in it. While the agreement was still just a draft, they could have come along at any moment with their own proposals. Those proposals that were up for adoption would have been adopted and those that were unacceptable would have been dismissed, but in a well-founded way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did President Milutinovic have an active role in the conclusion of this agreement on self-government in Kosovo and Metohija; if so, what exactly was his active role?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had an exceptionally active role. Of all the state officials, he was the one most seriously involved in this endeavour. He was involved, both in wording the actual agreement and later on, in trying to gain popular support for the agreement, in trying to advocate the solutions offered therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember whether President Milutinovic talked to the representatives of each and every ethnic minority in Kosovo? I'm referring to those that eventually signed the joint agreement.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talked to all of them, and he talked to the leaders of all the political parties that were part of the parliament at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Serbia's parliament you mean, in order to make sure he had their support, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was done in order to secure support, because when the government delegation was appointed it was said clearly that members of all parliamentary groups were invited to come forward with their own candidates to this delegation so that the Assembly might remain united on Kosovo and Metohija and on how to deal with Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what was the result of these efforts made by President Milutinovic, did he eventually garner any support from any courses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was support, except, as I said, for the Albanians, or rather, the majority parties; they decided to simply ignore the whole project.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when was the agreement signed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed in late November, in Pristina. A declaration was issued to mark the occasion. It was signed by the representatives of all the ethnic minorities that were involved in the drafting of the agreement, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the deputy prime minister to the federal government, Vladan Kutlesic, and I signed the document on behalf of the Republic of Serbia, I being the deputy prime minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular copy does not have any signatures. I thought I had seen a copy with signatures before. If we are going to be talking about that, I would prefer we use the signed copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe I had received one from the Defence but this one is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have in this bundle the original, the original part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The original of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is not the signed copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well it can't be the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be the original if it's not signed. I'm saying is the document itself not before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me -- just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can check a bit later and provide the document with the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, when the declaration was signed on the 25th of November in Pristina, was President Milutinovic there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, let us now move to 1999. Are you familiar with the principles of the Contact Group dated the 30th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 49, 1D018, page 414. Professor, you see the principles, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the non-negotiable principles, so-called non-negotiable principles, the fundamental elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it based on these principles or guide-lines that the meeting in Rambouillet was scheduled?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the principles based on which the talks at Rambouillet were to proceed. They were, as the document shows, non-negotiable. They were to be adopted as they were and possibly incorporated into any document that might have arisen based on the meeting between the two delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, throughout your many attempts to get in touch with the Albanians back in 1998, who in your opinion, or rather, what in your opinion was the crucial -- one crucial principle that you could not agree on?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key principle, due to which the representatives of the majority Albanian political parties did not respond to invitations to attend meetings, is the principle of the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and its neighbours, neighbouring countries, as well as the sovereignty of Yugoslavia. Therefore, it was that principle that did not suit Kosovo Albanians. And for those reasons most likely they did not take part, they did not respond to the invitations issued by government to attend 16 or 17 meetings, and they also refused to sign the principles offered by the Contact Group in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday we looked at the Security Council Resolution 1199 which referred to the territorial integrity and sovereignty of SFR Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I read it out yesterday, that portion of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The principles of the Contact Group, or rather, one of the principles of the Contact Group speaks of that issue as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the ten principles of the Contact Group is precisely that principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given that the meeting in Rambouillet was convened on the basis of these ten principles, one of which was the guarantee of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Serbia, do you have an explanation as to why the representatives of the majority Albanian parties did come to Rambouillet, in view of the fact that they obviously didn't want to accept that particular principle?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I think that they came to Rambouillet because they could not ignore the invitation extended by the international community, the Contact Group, that's on the one hand. And on the other hand, I think that they came because this agreement that was supposed to be reached in Rambouillet was only going to be a temporary one for self-rule in Kosovo and Metohija. And they were counting on having some manoeuvre space to actually challenge this principle or minimise it by way of including it in the provisional agreement, which would give them time subsequently to establish their long-standing desire; namely, that the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija decide about the fate of Kosovo and Metohija at a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the composition of the population in Kosovo and Metohija, if this referendum was to be held only in Kosovo and Metohija, the outcome would have been known in advance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. Albanians are an ethnic minority in the Republic of Serbia, but in Kosovo and Metohija, which is a part of the Republic of Serbia, they constitute a numeric majority. And this is what they were counting on whenever they insisted that the fate of Kosovo and Metohija be decided by votes of the people of Kosovo and Metohija, which is how they formulated it. There is no such notion as the people of Kosovo and Metohija. There are Albanians, Egyptians, Turks, Romani, Gorani, and so on, but there is no such thing as an aggregate category known as the peoples of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, when you were dealing with the non-negotiable principles, you referred to the refusal of the representatives of the main political parties -- or the main Albanian political parties to sign these principles. Was there some formal process through which the representatives of the Government of Serbia signed these principles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we did not talk directly to the Albanian delegation, which came there under the name of the Kosovo delegation, and it was a mono-ethnic delegation, comprising only Albanians, nobody else, we were unable to talk to them directly. So we conveyed to them via the mediating group consisting of three members that we would talk to them only if these non-negotiating principles were developed in the agreement. This is why we told the mediating Troika that these ten principles of the Contact Group be signed both by us and the Albanian delegation. Our delegation signed these ten principles and the Albanian delegation refused to do that, to sign them. And I think that in the documents you can find the text based on which you can see that we signed these ten principles, whereas the Albanian delegation did not, or rather, they explicitly refused to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have documents, Mr. Zecevic, that deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I was going in a chronological -- we will come to that in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, following these principles of the Contact Group, the principles established by the international community, a conference was convened in Rambouillet and our delegation, our government, received an invitation to attend the conference in Rambouillet precisely on the basis of those ten principles, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It was the National Assembly that decided that the delegation should take part in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please open tab 50, 1D443. Professor, would you please interpret and comment this document for us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this document contains the decision of the National Assembly concerning the participation of the delegation of the Republic of Serbia in negotiations on Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in which parts can we find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part 6, the last one. It says there that "pursuant to the invitation of the Contact Group to attend negotiations on Kosovo and Metohija on the 6th of February an invitation was sent to Serbia and the National Assembly decided to accept this invitation to attend negotiations because it is the firm orientation of the people and all political parties to try to achieve peace and to defend Kosovo and Metohija in every forum where the issue of Kosovo and Metohija is discussed anywhere in the world. By accepting these negotiations, we are making yet another step to contribute to the resolution of the problems by way of peaceful means. The National Assembly has authorised the government to designate a delegation that would attend the meetings." And in part 5, item 2, the National Assembly of Serbia formulated principles based on which the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija can be resolved successfully and permanently in the interest of everyone. These principles can be found in part 5, item 2. They were some sort of a compulsory terms of reference for the government when it came to appointing members of the delegation for negotiations in Rambouillet. If you have translation into English then I wouldn't go into these particular specific principles, but the key one was the last one which was discussed at length; namely, the principle that states that: "We do not accept the presence of foreign soldiers in our territory on any pretext of implementing the agreement reached."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is this the sort of response to these principles you're talking about, or is there a simple document that says, We accept every one of the non-negotiable principles?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. There is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because these principles are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These principles are the ones that have been adopted by the National Assembly of Serbia and upon the arrival in the Rambouillet as you will see, our delegation signed the ten principles and we have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say ten principles, there's a lot more than ten on the list in number 49. There's ten general elements --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ten general elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then there's at least that number in relation to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the general elements were accepted by the -- by the delegation of Serbia, the general elements, ten general elements, as the principles of resolving the Kosovo situation in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have read out to us the last principle adopted by the National Assembly, part 5, last item. Can you please explain to us why the National Assembly took such a position, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite natural for the National Assembly to take such a position. It is easily to explain. If we do reach an agreement on some issue, then we do not need foreign soldiers to enforce it. That means if the foreign soldiers are there, that means that the agreement is against somebody's will. An agreement reflects the meeting of the wills of the participants to the agreement, and if the parties agree to something then why would they need foreign troops on their territory to enforce, implement, that agreement? That's one thing. The other thing is the principle of territorial integrity and sovereignty is being acknowledged here as one of the principles. And it is incompatible with that principle to have the presence of foreign troops on our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The second point I understand entirely. On your first point, has your experience of events worldwide in the last 15 years altered that opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what particular experience you have in mind, but if the negotiating parties are serious, if they accept what they sign, if they accept it willingly, then why would the foreign troops need to enforce something that the parties had willingly agreed to on their own? Why would the foreign troops need to secure that? Foreign troops can secure an agreement or enforce it if somebody is against it so that they need to use force to ensure the implementation. But in that case, it is no longer an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, these conclusions reached by the National Assembly are, in fact, the mandate you are actually referring to a framework which -- within which the National Assembly as the highest organ of power gave authority to the delegation to participate in negotiations in Rambouillet, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. The National Assembly decided that Serbia needed to be represented in Rambouillet, and they did not give the delegation a carte blanche to do what they wanted in negotiations; rather, they specified in general terms several principles that the state delegation had to abide by. They could not violate those principles. And those principles had been previously used by the international community in their calls to participate in political dialogue by ways of political means, dialogue, peaceful mechanisms to resolve the crisis rather than an armed conflict. And then another principle was for respect for territorial sovereignty, full equality for all ethnic groups in Kosovo and Metohija without the possibility of anyone out-voting anyone else. In addition to that, the principles called for the application of solutions which were used in our constitution and in all international treaties concerning human rights. They called for autonomy in Kosovo and Metohija at the highest international level but within the framework of Serbia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And then another principle was that they did not accept the presence of foreign troops on the territory of Yugoslavia and they rejected firmly any attempts that would lead to secession of Kosovo and Metohija from Serbia. Except for this last one, all other principles were identical to those used by the international community in their appeals to solve by peaceful means the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija. Except for this last one, they used identical wording for their principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. As we were able to see, these conclusions were such that the National Assembly authorised the government to appoint members of the delegation. Would you please open tab 51, which is P0967. This is the decision published in the Official Gazette on the 5th of February, 1999, on appointment of the delegation to participate in the negotiations in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Official Gazette is the name of the publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And we can see here that you were appointed as head of the delegation, correct, that's in item 1?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Implementing the conclusions of the National Assembly that we have just commented upon, the government issued a decision appointing members of the delegation in France. I was appointed head of the delegation, and in addition to the presidents of the delegation, there were also 12 members. I'm now drawing your attention to the fact that it was a multi-national delegation, and that there were representatives of ethnic communities from Kosovo and Metohija representing absolute majority. Out of 13 members of the delegation, only four were Serbs. In addition to that, the delegation also comprised representatives of the federal organs, and those were Mr. Vladan Kutlesic, federal deputy prime minister; and Mr. Sainovic, also deputy federal prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a state delegation. This is not just Serbia's delegation. This is a delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave for France, the delegation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Arriving at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, the 6th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were the talks at Rambouillet opened on that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that evening the ceremonial opening of the talks took place. The talks were opened by the then-president of the French republic, Mr. Chirac and also the co-chairman of the Rambouillet conference Cook and Vedrine, Robin Cook and Vedrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did you get the first draft agreement, the first Rambouillet draft agreement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the first portions the next day upon our arrival at Rambouillet, the next morning, the 7th of February. There were three people involved in this particular round, Hill, Boris Mayorski, and Wolfgang Petritsch, they provided us with a framework agreement which is the first part of the agreement, as well as annex 1 containing a constitution for Kosovo. There was also annex 3 discussing appointments to bodies in Kosovo, and annex 6 which discussed the position of the ombudsman. We received this on the morning of the 7th of February in Rambouillet and this was given to us by the three chief negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said yesterday that Kosovo's draft constitution, which you refer to as annex 1 which you received in Rambouillet, is actually one of the versions of a document that you reviewed with Hill and O'Brien back in 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody gave us any explicit instructions in that regard but I was a party to the talks and I recognised it immediately. Constitutional law happens to be something I deal with on a professional basis, so I recognised many of the provisions from the countless plans drafted by Mr. Hill and Mr. O'Brien. I recognised many of those in annex 1 entitled a constitution for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you please go to 53, 1D122. This is your letter dated the 9th of February about these fundamental principles or general elements, if you like, which is something the Trial Chamber asked you questions about a while ago. Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we received these portions of the agreement, our delegation, of course, embarked on seriously studying these portions. We established immediately that some of the principles of the Contact Group were not envisaged in it or not fully envisaged. Some of those principles of the Contact Group that had been defined as non-negotiable, they were a given and they simply had to be implemented. That is why we decided to clarify the previous issue. What about the other party to these negotiations, does the other party accept these principles as non-negotiable at all? First of all, we had to ascertain that; this is the only way the talks could make any sense. If they refused to accept the principles that the international community had decided could not be changed or amended and were not negotiable, then the Rambouillet talks would turn out to be entirely pointless. It was for these same reasons that we asked for both delegations to agree to those principles and sign them so that we might embark on further efforts towards reaching an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This proposal that you made is to be found on page 2 of the document, it says "general elements," it's in English, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the principles established by the Contact Group. There are ten principles in total. They are listed here in the very same order that they were first worded in the original document produced by the Contact Group. To the left you see the Kosovo Albanian delegation, which constituted -- which consisted only of Albanian representatives. To the right you see the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, which as you see, unlike the previous one, was a multi-ethnic delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 54, 1D123. This is another letter you wrote on that same day in which I believe you requested a meeting for the basic principles to be signed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this letter reflects with regard to these principles is that we requested a face-to-face meeting with the Albanian delegation with no mediators. We wanted to thrash it out and see whether this delegation accepted these principles to begin with. My letter to the three chief negotiators was a part of these efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did that meeting ever materialise, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never did. The three chief negotiators informed us that the Albanians had refused to have that meeting. The entire agreement was envisaged as a series of talks, as a meeting between two delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you say the entire agreement, do you mean the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Rambouillet talks, the negotiations, were envisaged like that. They're called talks, talks meaning two delegations talking. Not only were there no such talks at the outset but no such talks ever materialised throughout our time there. Both parties talked to the chief negotiators. The parties never actually ended up talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, given the fact that the Albanian delegation refused to sign the basic principles, which were in actual fact the principles established by the Contact Group, you said a while ago to the honourable Chamber that our own delegation had signed the principles. When was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our delegation signed all of the principles, and we did that in Rambouillet on the 11th of February, 1999, all ten of the Contact Group principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please go to tab 55, 1D124. 1D124.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the Serbian version of the document that we have before us bears the signatures of each and every member of that delegation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is a statement by our delegation accepting the ten principles, based on which the Contact Group had scheduled this meeting, this conference, in Rambouillet. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is one thing that I wish to point out, though. This was all prompted by the co-chairman of the meeting, Mr. Robin Cook, the foreign minister of Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, does this clarify your question from before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, even after this did you still keep requesting meetings with the other party since, as you say, you had arrived there for talks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we persisted. At the various stages of our stay in Rambouillet and then in Paris, I as head of our delegation kept pressing the chief negotiators to organise a meeting between the parties. The chief negotiators, the three chief negotiators would always be there, needless to say, but I wanted a face-to-face meeting between the two delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 56, 1D094, this is your letter dated the 12th of February. In the meantime, as we can see from the letter, President Milutinovic had arrived in Rambouillet. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had arrived in the meantime, and in this letter I underlined the fact that he, too, is prepared to attend this meeting should all the other parties agree, of course, because formally speaking he was not a member of the delegation although he was the state president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was President Milutinovic there for the talks in the same capacity that he had previously travelled to Pristina for, to underline the importance attached to Serbia, first and foremost, to these talks. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely why he travelled to Rambouillet. This is a constitutional capacity of the president. He represents Serbia and expresses the unity of the state. But he was always earnestly involved in this entire effort in our attempts to talk directly to the delegation of the Kosovar Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when the delegation of Yugoslavia signed the ten basic principles or general elements established by the Contact Group on the 11th of February, you suggested that this move had been prompted by the co-chairman, Robin Cook. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is reflected in the document itself. It says: "a delegation appointed by the Government of Serbia at the meeting in Rambouillet prompted by the co-chairman, Robin Cook, Foreign Minister of Great Britain, wishes to release the following statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, while prompting the parties to do this, did the co-chairman specify whether they and the Contact Group still abided by the same principles for these talks in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they themselves had been members of the original Contact Group, and the whole talks in Rambouillet were organised around this. It was only natural for them to share the positions of a body to which they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these documents that you received from the three chief negotiators, from the representatives of the Contact Group, on the 7th of February, annex 1, 3, and 6, I believe --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- did you ever ask for the other, the remaining annexes to the Rambouillet agreement to be submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked to have the agreement in its entirety right away on the afternoon of the 7th of February. As a matter of fact, we had two general types of objections to the parts of the agreement that were an offer. The first set of objections had to do with the general elements of the Contact Group, since we had concluded that those had not been consistently complied with in those parts of the agreement that we received on the morning of the 7th. Secondly, in order for us to assess the wording of the agreement, we first needed to have the agreement in its entirety. To see what the agreement in its entirety was about and how all the various issues in the agreement were dealt with. Only then could we assess the agreement as a whole. I informed the three chief negotiators about this at our meeting, and then there was certain formal letters that we sent to them and which I signed as a head of the delegation. In these letters we requested to have the full text of the agreement so that we may be able to take a standpoint on the agreement as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 58, 1D096. Professor, is this one of the letters in which you request to have the full set of documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of those. It is signed in Rambouillet. I am here as head of the delegation, and I ask the negotiators to provide as soon as possible to the delegation designated by the Government of the Republic of Serbia all relevant documents intended for the Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The date on this document is the 12th, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did this on the 12th of February, but I think this wasn't the only time. There was another time. If you follow the time-line of these documents, I'm sure you'll find the other one that I'm talking about as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, at the outset the Rambouillet talks were supposed to go on for how long exactly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Contact Group initially had envisaged a week, that means the talks were to be concluded by the 13th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the deadline, the original deadline, was moved, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but not because either of the parties requested for the deadline to be moved. The reason was, even as late as the 13th of February, all we had were fragments of the agreement, very little of it, in fact, perhaps as much as a third. So the deadline was postponed because of the organisers, and it was moved from the 13th to the 20th of February, 1999, and then again no one else but the organisers themselves were to blame for another extension until the 23rd of February, 1999. Even as late as that we had not yet received the full text of the agreement, but rather just fragments by the 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that on the 13th of February, 1999, you had but a third of the agreement in your hands and still had no idea what the agreement in its entirety would amount to, even what the draft agreement would be, did you have any ideas at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had no idea about the substance, we had no idea about the general framework of what the agreement would comprise. We had the part of the agreement that concerned the ombudsman, but we didn't have the essential parts of the agreement. Even as late as the 13th of February, we still didn't have the essential parts -- oh, right, I do consider the constitution to be an essential part, but these were not the make-or-break points of the talks and we simply didn't have those in our hands. I was head of the delegation and I never actually held the text of the agreement in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when did you eventually receive the remaining documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parts of the agreement that I mentioned we received on the morning of the 7th of February, and then on the 13th of February, we received annex 4, entitled: "Economic Issues." According to what the Contact Group had first envisaged, the talks were to be ending on that day, and that was when we received annex 4. Later on, on the 15th, since the conference had been extended, on the 15th we received annex 4(A) entitled "Humanitarian Issues, Reconstruction, and Development."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I would intervene with permission. Now, Professor, learned Professor, please tell me besides these very formal invitations and meetings, were you also meeting informally over meals or dinners or something which opportunity would have provided -- which would have been an opportunity for at least meeting the other side informally and like they say, track two in diplomacy and so on to understand each other and to get to know of things? Or were you just being led by shepherds, who were the negotiators getting you together, getting you apart? What was really happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were led about shepherds, that's precisely how it was, but we did not act like a flock. We were quite aware what certain things meant. The two delegations were even physically separated. Our accommodations were on two separate floors of the castle at Rambouillet. We even dined, had lunch and dinner, in different dining rooms. Only a chance meeting in the hallway was possible, and even then they were unpleasant situations where, for example, I knew some colleagues, such as Professor Fehmi Agani, who was a university professor, and he would turn his head the other way. He felt uncomfortable, too, and he did that in order to avoid any possible conversation between us. I personally did not have any contact with any members of the Albanian delegation, even though I knew some of them from before. And we used to have, prior to that, a normal, professional communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor tab 60, 1D589.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we could have it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your letter to the negotiators dated the 16th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this letter to be exceptionally important for the course and nature of talks in Rambouillet. General public is not aware of the facts contained in this letter. When we received annex 4(A) on the 15th of February, I as head of the negotiation put an explicit question to the negotiating Troika whether the text of the entire agreement had been provided, had we finally received the entire agreement, because we had arrived on the 6th of February, and it was the 15th when I posed this question. The chief negotiators told me explicitly that that was the agreement in its entirety. So I referred to the answer I received from them in paragraph 1 of this letter. I say there: "Since you informed us at the meeting yesterday that we had finally received all annexes adopted by the Contact Group, including annex 4(A), we are now in a position to submit to you, in line with our concept, the single text of the agreement on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija with our comments and positions." So based on this letter, one can see that on the previous day the negotiating Troika had told us that we had the entire agreement in our hands. And based on that, we gave them back our comments, our views concerning the integral agreement, including all the annexes. That was the substance of this four-paragraph letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, if I understood you well, since the three chief negotiators, Mr. Mayorski, Petritsch, and Hill, submitted to you parts of the agreement and told you that that was the entire agreement, the delegation led by you prepared its own proposals and incorporated them into the text, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that, please. Mr. Zecevic, that is simply a repetition of exactly what the Professor has already told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember draft conclusions of the Contact Group on the 20th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 62, 1D674. Did this mean, these conclusions, that the deadline was extended by three days, as you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These conclusions extended the deadline for concluding the talks for the second time. It was extended this time by three days. The Contact Group said that the conference had to conclude by 1500 hours on the 23rd of February. Even when Contact Group issued these conclusions, we still did not have the entire Rambouillet agreement in our hands, more than half of it was missing, more than half of the text of the agreement was still missing. And one can see that in the numbers of annexes, number 2 was missing, number 5, and number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, please, do you remember what happened on the 22nd of February in Rambouillet, so the day before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of February -- are you referring to the letter which I sent out? I'm not sure what you are aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any attempts on the 22nd of February to give you some other documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. You know what? There was quite a lot going on in one single day. So when you asked me: Do you remember what happened on such and such day, I'm not sure what you have in mind because a lot of things happened on one single day as a rule. On the 22nd of February at 1900 hours, the negotiating troika brought to us precisely the missing annexes, annex 2, 5, 7, and 8. But annex 8 was an artificial product made out of the framework agreement in such a way that one particular article was set aside as a separate annex, and it was on changes to the agreement. And this was the greatest concession made to the Albanian delegation in order to have them sign the agreement. As head of the delegation, upon consulting the entire delegation, I refused to accept from the negotiating troika these annexes making a reference to their publicly-made statements that on the 15th of February we had the entire agreement in our hands. As it turned out, on the 22nd of February, at 1900 hours, we had by that time had only less than half of the agreement in our hands. And then the remaining part, the greater part, was given to us on the eve of the deadline for concluding the conference because we were told that it had to conclude by 1500 hours on the 23rd of February. We received at 1900 hours on the 22nd of February more than half of the agreement, the remaining part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, was that the only reason why you did not wish to accept these documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the main reason why we did not want to receive that. Naturally, we didn't know anything about the content of what they were offering because we didn't accept it, we refused to accept it, because the negotiators had gone back on their own word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is tab 63, document 1D97, dated the 22nd of February. In the text of the letter, you say that these documents were not accepted by Contact Group. Would you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the second reason why we did not accept the parts of the agreement that were offered to us, and we learned of its existence from one of the negotiators, Mr. Boris Mayorski. These particular annexes, 2, 5, and 7 were not adopted by the Contact Group at all, unlike the previous annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Professor. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, just continue.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So annexes 2, 5, and 7 were not adopted at all by the Contact Group. Annexes 2 and 7 were not even put on the agenda of the Contact Group. As for annex 5, it was discussed, but it's -- they did not decide on its adoption, and that was the second reason why we refused to accept annexes 2, 5, and 7. We formulated our objection in such terms that we said that those annexes were not only not adopted by the Contact Group but were not even put on its agenda. And the Contact Group was the organiser of the entire conference, that it was the Contact Group that formulated the agreement which was later submitted to negotiating sides for review.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, how did you know that this document was not discussed by the Contact Group, that these documents were not discussed by the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boris Mayorski stated so to us. He was one of the chief negotiators. And in the final text of the agreement that was submitted to us on the following day, he put next to his signature that he was signing on behalf of the negotiating troika, but he was signing to everything except for annexes 2 and 7. As for annex 5, he said that it was debated by the Contact Group but not adopted. He said that it was not put to the vote, its adoption, and he said that in the presence of other two negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was on the 22nd of February?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 22nd. On the 23rd of February, he put that in writing in the accompanying letter accompanying the integral text of the Rambouillet agreement. That was the integral text that we received on the last day at 9.00 in the morning. And as the Contact Group had decided, the conference was supposed to conclude at 1500 hours on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please turn to tab 65, 1D98. You see -- you see page 1, the date is 23rd of February, 9.30 a.m., is that the document that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. You can even see that I was wrong about the time. I said 9.00 and the document says 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as I can see from the last line of this document, you were given a deadline by which you were to respond.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given a deadline, a total of three and a half hours to provide our response. We were told to provide our response by 1.00 p.m., so they gave us three and a half hours to respond to more than half of the text, of the Rambouillet agreement, which we had seen at that point for the first time. What one can see here is the signature of Mr. Boris Mayorski, and then there is the added bit in handwriting, chapters 2 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was your understanding of paragraph 1 of the letter that you received, together with the comment underneath Boris Mayorski's signature? Paragraph 1 suggests that the documents were being presented to the delegations on behalf of the Contact Group or in the name of the Contact Group. What was your reading of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only way I could possibly have interpreted the document was that the name of the Contact Group was being misused. Something was being done in the name of the Contact Group that wasn't consistent with the nature of the Contact Group, specifically annex -- chapters 2 and 7, and yet the negotiators were suggesting that these were being submitted to us in the name of the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can read this for ourselves and see exactly what happened. Mr. Mayorski expressed his reservations, but he still signed the document before sending it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did sign it, but he did not sign chapters 2 and 7. And what we were told was all or nothing, the entire agreement but not parts of the agreement in isolation. There were parts that we would have agreed to, having amended them, especially the political portion. But what we were told was we cannot have parts of the document signed. We can either sign it and agree to it as a whole or not at all. Therefore, this is my interpretation of the signature in my capacity as a professional legal expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a good example of a useless answer and a useful answer. Your first answer to the question that Mr. Zecevic posed, which was a very sensible question, was simply to tell us the way you thought in which negotiations had been conducted. But much more important is the second answer you've given, which is about the pressure being put on you, which I anticipate is what Mr. Zecevic actually wanted to hear. So please try, Professor, to supplement the easily readable material in the answers that you give so we have the benefit of your personal insight into what happened. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the 22nd of February, Mr. Mayorski told you that the three documents, annexes 2, 5, and 7, had not been debated or agreed upon by the Contact Group. Did you ask him, or perhaps he just explained to you of his own accord, what exactly the three annexes were about that they were about to submit to you on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not ask for an explanation from Mr. Mayorski nor did he provide one of his own accord. He just told us about the status of those chapters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was it that said it was all or nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think as we go through these documents you will realise that later on in Paris this was exactly what was communicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- The agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer my question. You told us with three and a half hours to go you were told it was all or nothing. Who was it that told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Mr. Petritsch and Mr. Hill said this quite explicitly, and this was confirmed on several occasions, later on in Paris, that the agreement could not be signed in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of February, was that said by them in the presence of Mr. Mayorski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the position of the negotiating troika from the very beginning. This is what we were told the moment we arrived in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what -- when this -- well, I don't understand that answer. I'm asking you about what was said on the 23rd of February. Were you told then by -- well, sorry. Who were you told by on that occasion that it was all or nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All or nothing, Mr. Petritsch and Mr. Hill were saying that all the time, and I believe that to have been the position shared by the Contact Group as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. So it wasn't something peculiar to the 23rd of February, this assertion that it was all or nothing? This was a principle start to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right from the very outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That puts a different gloss on it, you see, Mr. Zecevic, when we get the full position. Anyway, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the 23rd of February at 9.30 a.m., you received annexes 2, 5, and 7. If you compare these to the documents already in your possession at that point in time, which you received on the 7th, 13th, and 15th, can you tell us what it was exactly that you received at 9.30 that morning, how much of it there was in view of the fact that the time you were given to respond was three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have here the full text of the Rambouillet agreement. If you just skim through it, if you look at what its size is, you can easily tell that it was more than a half of the full text. It appears that the text runs into 81 pages. If you add to that the pages contained in annexes 2, 5, and 7 and what that would amount to is more than the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you had three and a half hours to go through that and to state your position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, at the end of the Rambouillet conference on the 21st of February, you dispatched several letters, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 66, 1D582. Can you comment, please. Does this not suggest that after all you saw Rambouillet as a meaningful, positive effort, or am I simply wrong?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that Rambouillet was tantamount to some progress, progress towards some sort of a political solution. This is, above all, a reference to annex 1 and annex 3, possibly even annex 6, although the position of the ombudsman is politically neutral. Some progress had definitely been made. On the 20th of February, between the 19th and the 20th - and we had begun on the 19th - our talks with the negotiating team and their experts at about 1900 hours, and we remained in the room until 5.00 a.m. on the 20th working on the political aspect. This was the way forward. The only way was to work intensively and try to reach an agreement on the wording itself. But this is how long the single annex took, so that's something for you to bear in mind. And then on top of this the delegation of the Kosovar Albanians had to agree. Negotiators would have to go to them with the text, and then they were to provide their approval. Yes, progress was made, especially in the political sense regarding the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija. But we said what we had been saying all along. The only solution was in the possibility of a political dialogue. We agreed to continue the talks, but by doing something like this, by using this method, not trying to foist solutions on people, not trying to impose anything on other people, but rather by negotiating and by getting all the parties to voluntarily agree to certain solutions and getting both parties involved in direct negotiations if possible. We agreed to have the talks continue. We even granted our approval for Yugoslavia to review the possibility of an international presence in Kosovo and Metohija for the implementation of the agreement that was to be signed in Rambouillet. We did say that we did not want international soldiers to be there, but that did not rule out the possibility of having a presence of international civilian staff. And this thing was something that we were not able to negotiate because we had been told not to. We had been told that the presence of foreign international soldiers was out of the question for the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour, it's appropriate now to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Time again for a break, Professor. Please leave with the usher, as usual. We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one issue concerning tab 42, 1D91, if I may address it while the witness is preparing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a question of the original document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Well, Your Honour, the original document we don't have, the signed agreement we don't have; however, the declaration in support which refers to the document has already been admitted as 1D18, page 372, it's Professor Weller's book. So it has already been admitted on the 1st of March this year as an evidence. The declaration -- the declaration in support of the joint agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how does that resolve the matter of signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the declaration in support is signed and it has been admitted. And what our learned friend from the Office of the Prosecutor has actually seen is the page of Politika which we don't want to tender, which is, Your Honour, 47, 1D671, and you have it in your binder. That is probably the reason why Mr. Hannis saw -- he saw the signatures on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed -- oh, sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is 671 in already then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we are not tendering --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because that reflects the signatures, Your Honour, I don't have an objection then to that Politika coming in to reflect that because the witness has testified about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case we will move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit 1D671.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To assist the interpretation of tab 42, so now you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think just for the purposes of the record, tab 42 is 1D71 -- 1D91, I'm sorry, 1D91. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, are you aware of the declaration, or rather, statement of the Albanian delegation dated the 23rd of February, 1999, in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about this statement. It is 1D, or rather, tab -- it is tab 70, 1D018, 467 in your binder. That is point 34.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the delegation of the Kosmet Albanians considered as the focal point in the agreement, the last chapters -- rather, chapter 8 which came into being subsequently. Because this part on changing the agreement was taken out of the first framework agreement and turned into a separate text, and it says there that after a transition period expires of three years in Kosovo there would be a referendum by the people of Kosovo to decide on the fate of Kosovo. That is to say, that the Albanian delegation sees that part in the agreement as the most important one for them. That is to say, that out of the entire agreement which contains a provisional solution they see as the greatest value this possibility of after the expiry of the transition period the people of Kosovo will decide on the fate of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which indicates, I assume, what the objective of the Albanian delegation was at the talks in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were aware of that objective even as far as back as when we went to Pristina, and the proof that this is their objective is the fact that they never responded to the invitations of our delegation. Because it is not natural to talk to a state delegation about constituting another state in the territory of that same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, when did you find out about the existence of some bilateral letters and messages between the United States of America and the delegation of the Kosmet Albanians in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about that only after I returned to Belgrade, and after having read numerous books written by many authors about the negotiations in Rambouillet and Paris. That is when I saw many things which I as a participant in these negotiations had not known about. Inter alia, about those negotiations between the Kosmet Albanian delegation and Mrs. Albright.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Tell me, Professor, do you think that in relation to the scope of the mandate that the delegation had on the basis of the conclusions made by the highest authorities of Serbia, that is to say the National Assembly, dated the 4th of February, do you think that in relation to these conclusions your mandate, or rather, did you, the delegation, act fully in accordance with those provisions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes. And when we returned to Belgrade, we were not criticised at all for our positions or our conduct during the negotiations in Rambouillet, on the contrary. The work of the delegation was approved, and later the National Assembly adopted conclusions along the same lines; namely, that they expressed their satisfaction over the work of the delegation and expressed a high appreciation for the work of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, was the delegation prepared to accept the political agreement from Rambouillet or part of the political agreement from Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation was prepared, provided that some corrections were made in the offered text, and in the presence of Ambassador Petritsch, we incorporated these changes in the night between the 19th and the 15th -- the 19th and the 20th of February, 1999, in Rambouillet. That is to say that only Mr. Petritsch was present out of all the negotiators, and the expert team on our side consisted of Mr. Kutlesic and myself and two experts who were on our delegation, experts in international law, that is. And on the other side there was Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Etinski an associate of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "O'Brien," do you mean Mr. Jim O'Brien?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jim O'Brien.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is the same gentleman who during the course of 1998 came with Mr. Hill and talked to you in Belgrade and brought in different offers by way of an agreement on autonomy and self-government in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, did they believe at that time that your proposals were acceptable or did they give any comment whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had achieved a high degree of agreement, I must say, with the representatives of Mr. Hill. I assume that Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Etinski were the representatives of Mr. Hill or I don't know, I don't know their status. Maybe they were experts of the negotiating troika. A high degree of agreement, yes, but all of that was supposed to be approved by the Albanian delegation, too, they had to agree on it as well. As for this delegation, we had practically brought the text of the constitution to an end as was the political parts of the agreement. However, none of this was final. The Albanians had to agree to it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by the political part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The political part of the agreement is a colloquial reference that was usually made in Rambouillet, although this was not stated officially anywhere that that was a particular part of the agreement. That was the framework agreement. Then -- that's the constitution, then it's the part concerning elections, that is to say annex 3, and the part about the ombudsman. 4 and 4(A), annexes 4 and 4(A) are the economic part and part 2 has to do with the police, annex 2 is police and 5 and 7 are implementation. So, colloquially the jargon implied that the framework agreement was the political part as well as chapters 1, 3, and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, after the conference in Rambouillet was over, you, the delegation, returned to Belgrade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same day, during the night, after the press conference that was held at the Yugoslav embassy in Paris. It was held by the President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic. We returned during the night in Belgrade on the 23rd of February, the night between the 23rd and the 24th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during that press conference, that is 71, 1D586 in our documents here, so tab 71, 1D586, that's the document I'm referring to. During this conference, was the position you told us about just now repeated; namely, that the Yugoslav delegation was prepared to accept the political agreement from Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was repeated. And it was repeated in my letter as well, the one that I signed as the head of the delegation when the conference in Rambouillet was over on the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since this press conference was held by President Milutinovic, I assume that since he presented that position, since he uttered those words, he supported them, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is obvious, isn't it? I take into account what the honourable Presiding Judge said and I don't want to recount everything that is stated here, but you can see this in paragraph 4 of the transcript of the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, upon returning to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm -- bearing in mind what the Professor has just said, I'm trying to come to terms with the documents I have here under 71. There are --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- there are questions as well -- there's the statement itself, the press statement, and then do we have questions? Because I've -- we don't seem to normally have the Serb versions of these documents, but I've got a Serb version and almost at the bottom of the page number 5 it changes into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is why the CLSS didn't want to translate that because Mr. Milutinovic was actually responding in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, I see, I see. So the whole of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the relevant portion to which Professor was referring is the first -- this is the last paragraph on page 1 of the translation, continuing to page 2, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- translation has in -- in the upper -- upper part, it's bolded: "Press conference by Milan Milutinovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, upon your return from Rambouillet on the 23rd, if I understood you correctly, in the evening hours until the 5th of March, could you tell us what it was that was happening and what kind of information you had about the results as seen by the international community, the results of the talks in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not quite understand what it is that you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Belgrade on the 23rd of February, in the period of the seven days after that, there were lots of comments made by the international community, foreign media, local media, about the results of Rambouillet. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were comments. I don't know if this is what you had in mind, but it was mostly said that the demands were too great. In the press, including the foreign press, one could hear such statements, even by Mr. Kissinger who said that there is no government in the world who could have accepted what was offered in Rambouillet. Even one of the officials of the US state department said that the bar was raised too high on purpose so that they couldn't jump over it. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think -- just hold on a second. I take it there is a particular purpose behind that question because all of this for its content is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, I was laying down the foundation for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Favourable press comment would appear to be the foundation, so where do you go from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Markovic, please look at tab 74, 1D099, which is a joint letter from you and Mr. Milutinovic to Madam Madeleine Albright on the 5th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right, just put a specific question to me. So this is the letter that President Milutinovic and I sent to Mrs. Albright. I don't want to go into the content of the letter so as not to expose myself to criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the letter is self-explanatory. I think that you sent letters with the identical content to all members of the Contact Group and all core -- all co-chairs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A letter to Mr. Igor Ivanov? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Same date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Robin Cook?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hubert Vedrine?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joschka Fischer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, during the period between the two episodes of talks, was there any shuttle diplomacy being conducted by the negotiators or anyone else or were both sides simply left to sit and contemplate the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me about my personal experience, I had no participation in any such thing. As to whether that happened or not, I don't know.
