utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the letters that we just enumerated, you mostly presented your views and your position concerning the outcome of the talks in Rambouillet as well as the future talks which were supposed to be held in Paris, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you held the meeting with the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia on the 5th of March?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The delegation that went to Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the president of the Republic, Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please turn to tab 80, 1D748. Since we do not have the translation of this document, Professor, I will ask you to read out the relevant portions, which is on page 5, paragraph 2, the sentence commencing with the words: "We are prepared ..." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a public announcement, page 5, paragraph 2, the sentence beginning with the words: "We are ready, we are prepared ..."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We are prepared to commence negotiations in Paris and Belgrade and Pristina, anywhere where a political solution can be found. We ascribe absolute priority to that. In any place and around any table and in every meeting, we are committed for a peaceful -- to a peaceful solution for a broad autonomy within Serbia and Yugoslavia to equality of all ethnic communities."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was the public announcement following the meeting of the delegation attended by Mr. Milutinovic. Was this your joint announcement and your joint position, including President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the position of all of us attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, please give us your personal opinion. In your view, Professor, did Serbia want a political solution for the situation in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 since you were a direct participant in the talks and in all of the attempts to meet with the Albanians and you also know all the steps that were taken. Can you tell us this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to his personal opinion. He's not testified as an expert about this and his personal opinion is no better than yours or mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- the only difficulty I see with that question is the reference to Serbia wanting a political situation. If that was the Government of Serbia, then I couldn't see anything wrong with it because what we have here is a man heading the delegation appointed to do the will expressed by the Assembly. So on the understanding you're asking about the position of -- is it the government and Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the Serbian Assembly but the government --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think - and it's not that I think, I'm convinced - that the Government of the Republic of Serbia sincerely wanted for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija to be resolved, because the entire political life had been paralyzed, was burdened by the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. All those trips to Pristina support this. There were all those possibilities offered by the Government of the Republic of Serbia to hold talks. This is another confirmation of the position of Serbia. Furthermore, the efforts of the delegation in Rambouillet and the delegation appointed by the Government of Serbia following the decision taken by the National Assembly to send its delegation to Rambouillet are also a testimony of this. The delegation was prepared to even continue participating in the continuation of talks in Rambouillet. So all of those meetings that were scheduled and the participation in the international conference acceptance of the general elements offered by the Contact Group and signatures underneath those elements are all a testimony of the fact that all that was needed for an agreement to be reached was the consent of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, when did the delegation go to Paris again for continuation of the talks, do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 14th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, President Milutinovic also travelled to Paris, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, President Milutinovic was present in Paris throughout the entire time, unlike in Rambouillet where he attended only the second portion of the talks starting on the 10th, the greater part of the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please look at tab 82, 1D587.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say 82?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 82, 1D587. This is the statement by President Milutinovic on the 16th of March in Paris. Professor, do you remember that Milan Milutinovic said: "I emphasise that we are ready to accept the political portion of the agreement"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is in compliance with his initial statement given in Rambouillet back on the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. On the 17th of March, you wrote a letter to the negotiating troika. This is tab 84, 1D110, dated the 17th of March, 1999. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us, what did you seek by way of this letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in Rambouillet, this letter represented an appeal to the negotiators to organise a joint meeting of the two delegations, and we explained the reasons for that; namely, so that in a direct dialogue one could hear the comments and opinion of the other side about our proposals, rather than hearing from negotiators what they had to say about the opinion of the other side, rather than having them convey to us the opinion of the other side, no. We wanted to hear straight from the other side what they thought of our proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, Ambassador Nikola Cicanovic was a member of the delegation or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was the secretary of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 85, 1D111, you can see his letter there to the co-chairs dated the 17th of March, 1999. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, very well. This is our request that we put forward in Paris; namely, we wanted some sort of a rule to be established that would regulate the work of the conference, rules of procedure, because the conference in Rambouillet unfolded in a random way without any sort of a plan. One didn't know what was happening when, nor was the form of anything established. So we wanted some sort of rules of procedure to be specified as to how the conference would unfold, how an agenda would be formulated, how to submit written proposals, and so on. Everything that generally needs to be done in a conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When Mr. Cicanovic refers in that letter to experts, is he referring to civil -- is he referring to state officials who were there to deal with particular issues on behalf of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Our delegation in Paris did not have experts. We only had them in Rambouillet. Most likely, he had in mind Mr. Kutlesic and myself because we were quite involved in the expert portion of the work. That's what we were mostly involved in finding proper wording. That's what Mr. Cicanovic was referring to because there was no other experts there. Mr. Etinski and Mr. Mitic were present in Paris and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what are they -- sorry, they were in Paris. You said there were experts in Rambouillet, what do you mean by experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Etinski and Mr. Mitic were there. One of them is a retired official of the Ministry of the Interior. He's no longer alive, unfortunately, and Mr. Etinski, at the time, I believe was legal advisor in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Both of them were experts for international public law. As for the Albanian delegation, they refused for the experts to meet in Rambouillet because there was such proposals. We wanted these two experts of ours to meet with their experts, that's what we proposed, and the Albanian delegation rejected that. And since these people were practically not used in Rambouillet, they did not go to Paris because Mr. Kutlesic and I, professionally speaking, had the proper training for that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we all heard about the results of the Paris talks. What I want to know now is one thing specifically. Professor, what about President Milutinovic, during his stay in Rambouillet and in Paris, did he ever at any time try to obstruct the negotiations in Rambouillet first and then in Paris?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has been amply demonstrated so far. Quite the contrary, in fact. Each and every statement he made whenever he attended any meetings, what he contributed was exactly the opposite. You see he stated at the very outset of the Paris conference: We are prepared to accept a political solution. This is not the sort of statement made by a person who does not wish to contribute meaningfully to a conference or to a round of negotiations. This person is not out to obstruct; he's out to enhance the process. That much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I should assume that you saw President Milutinovic on a daily basis during your stay in Rambouillet and then in Paris and also previously back in 1998, when you worked together on drafting the documents submitted by Mr. Hill and by Jim O'Brien, as well as during the three joint visits with the president. Did you ever see or hear President Milutinovic voice any sort of desire for war, for the use of force, in order to resolve the Kosovo issue or was it exactly the opposite?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exactly the opposite. The views that he voiced were exactly the opposite of what you have just suggested. We talked about the 18th of March declaration issued by the president of the Republic back in 1998. The main point of the entire declaration was this: The only way forward for Kosovo and Metohija, the only way for the crisis to be resolved, is a political dialogue between the two sides, between all of the sides, and that is the political gist of everything he ever stated. This one sentence, there wasn't a single time he addressed the public without reiterating this one thing, this one sentence, being repeated over and over again, this one crucial thought. But it's also about his convictions, this was a matter of conviction for him. I'm certain based on my communication with President Milutinovic that this was his inner-most conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your capacity as deputy prime minister and head of the delegation for talks with Kosovo Albanians back in 1998, in your capacity as chair of the Rambouillet delegation and the Paris delegation, head of the Paris and Rambouillet delegation, did you ever hear President Milutinovic, or indeed anyone else, saying they thought it was a good idea to have the Albanian population driven out of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Each and every one of their statements make a point of underlining that the Kosovo question could only be resolved by getting all the ethnic minorities to agree. The Albanian ethnic minority always comes first in each and every one of these statements since it also happens to be the most voluminous community, ethnic community in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you ever hear President Milutinovic say anything along these lines, or perhaps someone else commenting on Milutinovic's words, something to the fact of Yugoslavia being subjected to bombings, to air-raids, would lead to a massacre in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So nothing like that was ever uttered in Rambouillet, for example?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even there. I attended every single meeting that President Milutinovic attended at the time. I am still under oath, the oath that I took last Monday, and I state with full responsibility that President Milutinovic never at any of the meetings uttered those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did anyone from the negotiating troika, Mr. Petritsch, for example, ever complain to you that Mr. Milutinovic or anyone else had told him that any air-strikes would necessarily lead to a massacre in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the negotiators ever approached me to complain about anything like that. However, my work with the negotiators was on the wording of the agreement, and that was the gist of all of our communication. Most frequently, I spoke with Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Etinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what about the issue of Kosmet's independence. Isn't that in a manner of speaking the one great issue, the issue of all issues, the paramount issue, the issue to end all issues?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians unequivocally demonstrated just that. I'm not talking about the more recent history. I'm talking about what I was involved in at the time, the attempts to negotiate in Pristina and then subsequently Rambouillet and Paris. I'm absolutely convinced that for the Albanian side there is no alternative to independence in terms of resolving the Kosmet situation. I'm absolutely positive and I have no doubts whatsoever about that based on my two-year intensive study of the issue in my capacity as Serbia's deputy prime minister, in my capacity as head of the talks delegation, and as head of the Rambouillet and Paris delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, how do you feel about this? Had this question been ruled out based on your knowledge of all these facts and you were directly and personally involved, could there still have been some sort of a political solution that would have resulted from these talks with the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A political solution would have implied that Kosovo and Metohija did not become independent, an independent state. I don't think the Albanians would have agreed to that. They hadn't signed the agreement before this chapter was introduced, or rather, this annex, annex 8, chapter 8, formulating the possibility that the eventual status of Kosovo and Metohija would be decided at an international conference, taking into account first and foremost the will of the people living in Kosovo and Metohija. As soon as they heard this, both in Paris and in Rambouillet, they interpreted this to mean plebiscite on the independence of Kosovo and Metohija; that was their instantaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, following your return from the Paris talks, you submitted a report to the People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our job to do that because we had been appointed by that same Assembly to conduct the talks. We had to settle up in a manner of speaking, and we had to have our work evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The session was held on the 23rd of March, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 90, 1D032. Page 4, that's your report, page 4, page 5, through 14. In the English page through -- page 5 through 12. There is no need to go through your reports; it's in our binder and you have confirmed its authenticity for us. In this report you state all these facts, which you have stated today before the Trial Chamber, as well as the conclusions that we discussed a while ago. Is that not right, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: President Milutinovic also spoke at this Assembly meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there throughout and he asked to take the floor. He contributed to the discussion that ensued after the report had been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you heard what President Milutinovic had to say on the occasion, and I suppose there were other occasions when he spoke in the Assembly or when he addressed the public. Did President Milutinovic ever express any sort of radical nationalist views calling for the use of force, war, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the entirety of his public statements, you can't find a single example of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that applies to the 23rd of March, 1999, as well, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. If you look closely at what exactly he said, you can arrive at the conclusion yourself quite easily, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you listen to President Milutinovic's contribution in the Assembly on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He outlined his own views on the situation, the general situation, the Paris/Rambouillet talks, the various requests that were made to Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were, yourself, a party to these talks at both Rambouillet and Paris. In your view, did President Milutinovic mislead the People's Assembly by what he said in the Assembly on the 23rd of March, 1999? Was his contribution misleading in any way in terms of misstating facts or stating things that weren't facts or providing inaccurate information on the substance of the talks or what the actual problem was that was at stake?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was physically present, and you also have the record of that discussion. Anyone can have a look and see for themselves. There is absolutely no need for me to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I would like you to comment. After all, you are the one who is best-placed to know. You were involved in the negotiations and talks yourself. You have direct knowledge of all of this. The delegates listening to President Milutinovic in the Assembly did not have the same sort of knowledge that you did.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no elements whatsoever -- do you mean this contribution specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this contribution specifically.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see nothing in this contribution to suggest anything like that. We're talking about the People's Assembly. There are 250 delegates. Not all of them have the same level of education. This was not meant to be some sort of a dry speech given by a legal expert, an expert on international relations. This is the sort of address that was perfectly suited to the environment that it was given in. This is common language being used to convey a message to the delegates so that they understood what exactly had gone on in both Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Professor, after the close of discussion, the People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia as its supreme body adopted a decision and some conclusions, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was based on the report and the ensuing discussion that the People's Assembly adopted a number of conclusions. They had adopted a number of conclusions prior to our departure, and the same thing happened following our return and our report. New conclusions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go to tab 91, 1D033, sir. Is this the decision? Are these the conclusions that were eventually published in Serbia's Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you were in the Assembly that day and you submitted a report too. Do you remember the exact majority adopting these conclusions and this decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that it was a sweeping majority. I think a total of three or four delegates abstained, no more than that. I am, however, now relying on my memory. My memory's imperfect and it has been eight years since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, we can go back to the record and see for ourselves what the figures were, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite certain that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking about what you remember.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember, let me tell you this: I filed my report. I didn't exactly count the votes, but that was the general atmosphere that prevailed in the Assembly. It was one of universal acceptance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, during the bombing, the NATO intervention against Serbia in 1999, you were still deputy prime minister, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was deputy prime minister all the way up to the point when a political agreement was reached on the 16th of October, 2000, establishing a mechanism for the transfer of power to the new government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during those 78 days, the Government of Serbia sent to President Milutinovic a number of decrees that you spoke of during the first part of your testimony as an expert. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. As a matter of fact, I even signed some of these documents as deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please open tab 92, 1D144. Professor, this decree has to do with the personal identification cards during a state of war. Would you like to have a look at this? Is that correct? Is that what it pertains to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You signed this letter sent to President Milutinovic, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Attached thereto is the text of the decree as well as the explanation for it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony as an expert, we heard your comments as to the reasons for passing this decree and the text of the decree that was published in the Official Gazette. That is 1D144. Do you remember that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the text that you submitted as attached to this letter is identical to the text that was published in the Official Gazette and what we saw in 1D144. It's just that the president signed the ordinance on passing this decree with this kind of substance.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance, the content, was determined by the government and the president of the republic on the basis of the proposal made by the government, the president signed this, promulgated it, and this is in accordance with Article 83.7 of the constitution, which we commented upon the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember what the total number of decrees submitted to the president was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, 16 decrees were submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And all of these decrees contain proposals made by the government have actually identical -- the identical kind of form like what you signed. You sent a letter with a proposal of the text of the decree to the president, including an explanation as to why it was necessary to pass such a decree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I as deputy prime minister signed those that were from the realm of my responsibilities, and that was legislation and the legal system. As for those pertaining to the economy and the economic system were signed by the other deputy prime minister who was in charge of that particular field and entrusted to do so by the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are these 16 decrees, tabs 92 through 101, and then from 103 to 110. Professor, during 1999, were you present at this meeting between President Milutinovic and President Rugova?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this took place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at 1D -- no, no, sorry about that. Tab 101, tab 101, P00416, that is the joint statement by President Milutinovic and Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There are details involved. What did you say? 101? Was that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 101, P00416, signed joint declaration by the late Dr. Ibrahim Rugova and President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was during the bombing of Serbia, and I remember that it was with great difficulty, at the risk of our own lives, we travelled from Belgrade to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "you," in the sense of we, you mean yourself and President Milutinovic, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember any particular details concerning this meeting, which as far as I can see here was held on the 28th of April, 1999, what was the atmosphere of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the meeting unfolded in a constructive atmosphere, if I can put it that way. Mr. Rugova was a reasonable man. He understood the seriousness of the situation that the country was facing, and in a few paragraphs it was established what it was that was to be done by way of political moves in the newly created situation. So it was established here, it was concluded here, that yet again efforts should be renewed for a political dialogue, that negotiations should be direct. That representatives of the international community could attend negotiations based on mutual consent, but in the capacity of guests, having learned from the experience of intermediaries in Rambouillet and Paris. And finally, to establish as soon as possible an organ that would act as a transition government, but primarily to resolve burning humanitarian issues at the time. So that was the provisional Executive Council of Kosovo. Those were the main points in these talks. It was my impression that Mr. Rugova sincerely and as a human being wanted to find a solution to the newly created situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Professor, whether Dr. Rugova on that occasion made a present -- gave a present to President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but in view of the ban on presents, I don't want President Milutinovic to be held responsible for something else. He got a present from him, a mineral sort of, a crystal mineral, in a box and he was very hospitable in that situation. The country was being bombed and there were signs of the bombing all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you were present when they made a statement for television, you stood there by them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was standing there, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I have one more question, one or two questions, rather, and I think that we will be done.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome. Professor, a moment ago you spoke about statements made by President Milutinovic. I asked you about that I'm interested in your opinion about the character of Mr. Milosevic, who's a person you know who you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the interpreter misspoke, it's not Milosevic, it's Milutinovic. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The character of Mr. Milutinovic -- well, can you say what you have to say. I don't want to lead you in any way in giving an answer.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I can say to you specifically. President Milutinovic came to that office with a great deal of diplomatic experience. In that sense, he was an untypical politician, probably because of that kind of experience and because of his nature, he was very open to agreement, negotiations, dialogue. He was never in favour of any kind of dictat, any orders, issuing orders, carrying things out without any comment, anything that he may have said; so a person with whom one could reach agreement and was always ready to hear out the other side and to talk in a civilised manner to people who had different views.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In order to illustrate what you said just now, can we look at tab 111, 1D642, agreement on parliamentary elections in the Republic of Serbia, early parliamentary elections. All of this is being done at a very serious moment for Serbia in October 2000. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This was a decisive, crucial move that was made and the transfer of government, transfer of power that occurred in the Republic of Serbia in the month of October of 2000. This was a far-reaching step, and I'm certain that this prevented political conflicts which would not have ended only on the political scene but they might have escalated and reached the proportions even of a civil war. This was one of the most critical moments in the evolution of Serbia from the moment when it adopted a multi-party system in 1990 and from the moment it was constituted as a multi-party parliamentary democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, President Milutinovic - how should I put this? - managed to find a compromise even with his bitter political opponents to find a solution that prevented bloodshed in Serbia, as you had put it, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy, I just wanted to put an objection on the record at this point. This evidence -- the same objection I made regarding the introduction of the letter from ex -- former President Djindjic. I don't think this is material to the issues in the indictment. I understand it may go to mitigation at some point in time, but I don't think it's relevant to the issues in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it does go to mitigation, of course, it has to be led at this stage. So please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you heard my question. On that occasion President Milutinovic was the one who managed to find with his bitter political opponents a compromise and a solution which avoided bloodshed in Serbia, civil war at any rate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, proceeding from a conviction that the then-government in Serbia that was quite constitutional and legal and the National Assembly, that was also quite constitutional and legal, no longer had legitimacy because of the new balance of political power, although according to the constitution this government still had a mandate; its term of office had not expired, and the Assemblies, too. President Milutinovic talked to the leaders of the opposition and the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Vojislav Kostunica, and he together with him was a guarantor of this agreement. He established that the existing government would resign, although it was quite legal and constitutional. There were no objections in terms of constitutionality that could have been voiced against this government. So this government would resign, a transitional government, a provisional government, would be elected from among the signatories of this agreement. This government would propose to the president to dissolve the National Assembly, then the president would dissolve the National Assembly, and a new National Assembly would be elected, which would be legitimate in relation to the existing political constellation, the balance of political forces that was in place. And then that Assembly would in turn elect its own government. This was the Assembly that was elected on the 23rd of December, and it elected a government and Mr. Zoran Djindjic remained prime minister. So the mandate of the Assembly was still in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I just wanted you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mandate both of the Assembly and of the government was still in place. Their term of office had not expired, but in order to forestall any kind of political enmity and unrest that could escalate, in order to prevent that, this is the move that was made in order to prevent that and to make it possible for there to be a transfer of power in the Republic of Serbia along a legitimate track. I was deputy prime minister in that government, and the prime minister then was Mirko Marijanovic, and he had resigned on the 16th of October because this agreement had been reached. So according to our constitution, according to the constitution of 1990, once the prime minister resigns, the mandate of the entire government ceases; and I was deputy prime minister in that government. A provisional government was elected. It proposed to the president to dissolve the Assembly. The president dissolved the Assembly and new parliamentary elections were about to be underway. This showed that as far as the president of the Republic of Serbia is concerned and also the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that they were up to their constitutional office; that is to say that they embodied state unity, that they in a way were organs with the highest level of legitimacy after the Assembly. So they proposed -- they proposed that the existing authorities, because it was believed that there was no legitimacy, that they should interrupt their mandate and that the new political forces be given a chance to elect new organs of government. So as you asked me about this move of President Milutinovic, we see those characteristics of his personality and of his character, the ones that I spoke about a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just one more question. This entire transition was carried out in accordance with the laws in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This transfer of power was in accordance with the then-constitution that was in force; moreover, that constitution remained in force for another six years. So it wasn't Milosevic's constitution, as it was referred to, no. It was in force for another six years for the new government. And it wasn't until last year in November of 2006 that Serbia adopted a new constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, two tabs we encountered I think which were not translated, tab 17, tab 80. From 17 you read the -- or you had the Professor read the relevant part, therefore it does not need to be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think for tab 17 there should be an extra -- there should be a translation, and it might be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the translation is pending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, yeah. So it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one other matter about your exhibits. You haven't referred to them all, so what's the position in relation to the ones you skipped over?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as our witness has adopted it in 92 ter statement, I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so does the 92 ter statement list everything here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you doing -- is it listed paragraph by -- are they all listed paragraph by paragraph or are you relying to any extent on the annex, I think, which is the index for these --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The annex is basically the very same list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Except that it doesn't have tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he does refer within his 92 ter statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To all these documents which are contained in this list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- before you get to the annex?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, can you remind me what 1D671 is. Was that the -- it was the Politika article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- does that require to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think the other exhibit he showed is the English of what appears in Politika. The only difference is Politika has the signatures for us to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in these circumstances it remains as we decided earlier admitted without need for you to submit any further translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because the previously admitted document, the 1D18, the Professor Weller book actually cites the whole declaration word by word in English. This is -- basically, this is just for the purposes of photography because it has the signatures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a suitable time for us to adjourn for our lunch break. Professor, please go again with the usher. We will resume at 1.45, when you will start the cross-examination by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.42 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My name is Tom Hannis, and I will be asking you some questions. I want to ask you about your report, but before I do that, I think, while you've still got the red binders there I want to ask you a couple of questions about the decrees that were issued during the war. If you could turn, sir, to what are tabs 92 through 95 in your red binder, and that is exhibits 1D144, 147, 150, and 153. You're familiar with those, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, these are the four decrees that the text for the decrees that ultimately issued, as well as the statement of reasons, were I guess prepared by you or delivered through you to Mr. Milutinovic for the signature and issuance. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was formulated by the government at its session, the Government of Serbia, because the government is the one that establishes the proposal. I as deputy prime minister in charge of legislation signed it on behalf of the government, and in the accompanying letter you see that the Government of the Republic of Serbia at the 83rd Session in April of 1999 formulated the following proposals. So the government formulated this, and I signed it on behalf of the government. Later on, it was submitted to President Milutinovic for promulgation and the promulgation itself was announced in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say the government met in a session on this matter, how many people are we talking about? Is that the five deputy prime ministers and the prime minister or is that some bigger group?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This involved the entire government, the entire cabinet. The cabinet had 30-something members, and in its plenary session cabinet adopted all decisions. That was the only possible way. The government could only issue decisions in sessions where they had a quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often were they meeting during the first two weeks of the NATO bombing, did they meet on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, cabinet held sessions once a week; however, whenever necessary they would meet more often. As far as I remember, at that time the sessions were held two or three times a week because the country was being bombed and it was very dangerous for the cabinet to meet frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where the meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially the sessions were held in the government building in Nemanjina 11. However, since that building was bombed and destroyed, subsequent sessions were held in the building of the national bank of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With respect to these four decrees, I see that -- it appears to be what's a cover letter to President Milutinovic, and it seems as though the identical cover letter was prepared and a copy attached to each of the four separate decrees, with a circle being drawn around the number of, I guess, the particular decree to which it pertained. Do you recall is that how it was done?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There was a cover letter accompanying the text of the decree and then there was also the statement of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the date on the top of the page on each of these appears to be the 6th of April. So I take it, is that the day that you signed it and that it would have been delivered to President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the day when I signed the letter. Now, whether it was delivered to President Milutinovic on the same day, I truly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is less of an objection more of a technical point. If counsel is going to refer to multiple documents as he has now to each of these, it would be helpful if he at least gives the exhibit numbers so they can be on the e-court. Because none of the Defence counsel have any of these binders that the Judges and Prosecution apparently have. So it's impossible for us to follow all this and I fear we're going to get lost in the midst of all this as we try to look up these documents, when we start referring to multiple documents that we don't have in front of us, that we have to seek on e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis has, in fact, given you the numbers as well as the tab numbers and we've only been referring to the first of these so far. So he'll no doubt bear in mind to refer to each of the others as he goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour 1D144 is the one that's on the screen I understand, and these letters are identical except, as I indicated, the four documents that are listed on 1, number 2 is circled, that's on 1D144. And the others have either 1, 3, or 4 circled, but the text of each letter is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markovic, you don't know when these would have been delivered to Mr. Milutinovic, whether it was the same day or later?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- do you know how it was delivered and by whom?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either with any certainty. I can only speculate. These are technical issues after all, and normally deputy prime minister doesn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In relation to where the government met in their sessions, where was Mr. Milutinovic's office, was it in the same building, a block away, nearby?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of President Milutinovic was always in the same place and that place was not bombed, it was in Andricev Venac. That building was not far from the government building which was bombed, and it was a bit further away from the building of the National Bank of Serbia, which is where the government held its sessions subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to your signature on each of these four cover letters, beneath the text on the left side of the page it appears there's another signature and the date of 6 April. Do you see that on your version?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't decipher this. I wouldn't be able to tell you with any certainty because the signature is not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall if that signature was on the document at the time you signed it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was there when I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I assume, professor, as a deputy prime minister you weren't yourself actually physically preparing these documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who did that with regard to these four?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by the secretariat of the government pursuant to the decision taken by the government in one of its sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the individual who actually did that hands-on work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the secretary of the cabinet was a lady called Zivka Knezevic and deputy secretary of the cabinet was Mrs. Mira Djurekovic. I don't think that these are their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when these four decrees were actually published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the text in front of me several days ago when I was interpreting it here before the Trial Chamber. I wouldn't be able to tell you when they were actually published, but I did have this in my hands in examination-in-chief when answering the questions of Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at -- we'll look at another document in a minute that may help us with that, but before we move on I want you to look at 144, that's tab 92 for you. The second page in that document is the actual decree on personal identification cards during a state of war. And that page has the date of 31 March 1999 and President Milutinovic's name on it. Is that how it appears on your copy -- I'm sorry, Professor, I may have misled you. When I said number 144, I was referring to our exhibit number in court. It's tab 92 for you. Do you have that? Yes, I think it's the second page.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the actual decree itself with President Milutinovic's typewritten name at the bottom at any rate is dated 31 March 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Well, my explanation is -- yes. It says here the 6th of April too. I thought that the government held its session and then subsequently sent this to President Milutinovic, but now I see that there's a difference in dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what my question was about. Do you know why the decree itself has the date of 31 March, which is six days before the date on the cover letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to explain this, but one needs to see when this decree was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia. You know what, the country was in the state of war. It was impossible to keep orderly records. The secretariat of the government was moved to another building, somebody else's building. So it's possible that such errors crept up because the administration did not work under normal circumstances. There were air-raids, air sirens going on constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you put up Exhibit P993, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, do you see that on the screen in front of you? Sorry, I don't have a hard copy for you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to the page with the identification cards, the first English page it was up. I'm not sure which e-court page it is in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, can you see the cover page for that issue of the Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My Cyrillic's not that good, but that looks like the 7th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go I think to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I think it's item 306 is the law on identity cards.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There in the Official Gazette it has that date of 31 March 1999. Let me ask you a question about how the process works. When you on behalf of the government proposed this decree and forwarded it on to President Milutinovic, what does he do with it? Does he actually sign it? Do you know happens between the time it leaves your hands and the time it actually appears in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once it leaves the cabinet, President Milutinovic signs the decree, and then it is sent to the Official Gazette to be published. This is the path that a decree travels within the channels of the Government of Serbia before it is published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, waiting for translation. Sir, do you know what happens with the copy that the president signs? Where is that kept once he signed it? Is it kept in an official archive? In his office? Where would it be?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speculate that it is kept in the archives of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the end of his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was there a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter seems to have missed part of your last answer. Could you repeat that answer, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely it is kept in the archives of the government and in the archives of the president of the republic. But when it comes to these administrative issues, I'm not knowledgeable about them because members of the cabinet did not deal with such issues. It was the secretariat that dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to tab 92, Exhibit 1D144, the decree on identification cards, do you know who actually drafted this decree? That wasn't you, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Drafts of decrees, or rather, of all enactments are prepared by the relevant ministry. In this case, it was done by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who in the Ministry of the Interior would have drafted this particular one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Professor. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The last couple of days the witness has said that anything relating to the Ministry of Internal Affairs is beyond his expertise and now we're getting a question for him to speculate who in the Ministry of Internal Affairs would have done X, Y, and Z. I think that we're getting afoul of the witness's capacity to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness is perfectly able to tell us the extent of his knowledge and to know the difference between that and speculation, so we will allow the question to be answered. Professor, do you know who in the ministry would have drafted this particular order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In every ministry there was a service dealing with regulations, and that service normally created drafts of regulations adopted by the government, all laws that the government prepared as its proposal for the National Assembly. So this was a service drafting regulations, but only within the competence of every ministry. In addition to that there was a government secretariat for legislation, and every draft regulation had to pass through that secretariat, every draft submitted to the government at its session. And the secretariat had to approve it, approve it in the sense that they would check whether it was in compliance with the constitution and the legal system and to see whether it was valid in the legal technical sense of the word, but they did not go into the content of such drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it the -- well, I don't know. Let me ask you. The statement of reasons supporting the proposed decree, is that drafted by the same office or same individuals that wrote the substantive content of the decree or is there a separate department that would deal with reasons?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same service that wrote a draft regulation also writes the statement of reasons for that draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this particular decree, and I guess the others as well, by -- by looking at them it appears that they're intended to apply throughout the entire Republic of Serbia, including Kosovo and Metohija, yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. According to the constitution, the Republic of Serbia is a single legal territory. The regulations adopted by the state organs of the Republic of Serbia are considered valid in the territory of the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us a little bit yesterday I think about the changes, the differences, between this law and the previous Law on Identification Cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe that's Exhibit P1832, if we could put that up, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I have this listed as tab 27, but I don't know if it's 27 in the red binder or in the blue binder. If, perhaps, Mr. Zecevic could assist.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope I wrote the number down. It may have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is -- Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, it is at tab 28 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the red binder or the blue binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The blue binder, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My register is grey, it's neither red nor blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 28 of the grey register.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies, Professor, I think I'm the only one who had blue. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that some of the differences were that there was a reduction in the age from 18 to 14, yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you also indicated there was a change in the requirements about how one went about getting an identity card, if they no longer had theirs, in the new law. But could you look at Article 23 in the old law, that's Exhibit P1832 or tab 28 for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to I think it's the last page of this document that has Article 23. And can we have the English up as well, it's page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I reading that correctly, Professor? That seems to say that the Law on Identity Cards, the old Law on Identity Cards, applied throughout the territory of the republic outside the autonomous provinces and in Vojvodina. As I read that, it seems it does not apply to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are entirely right. This is a law that was adopted in 1974, under the 1974 constitution. And there was, indeed, the sort of regime in place in terms of the division of legislative powers between the Republic of Serbia on the one hand and the province on the other. There is reference here to Article 301 of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, however, as far back as in 1990, the constitution ceased to apply. The 1974 constitution has 136 articles, therefore it's impossible to invoke Article 301. I think this Law on Identity Cards was followed on another Law on Identity Cards that was in compliance with the 1990 constitution. This law was adopted in 1974 when the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia was in force and that's the name of the Official Gazette, too, the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, when it still was a socialist republic, and that was for as long as 1990. Back in 1990, it became the Republic of Serbia, and when the new constitution was adopted the old 1974 constitution ceased to apply. This law was passed under the 1974 constitution and it had to be made consistent with the new 1990 constitution. I'm not sure about the number of the Official Gazette, when these -- when this law was published -- in which this law was published. Other than that, you are entirely right in what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created, do you know was there -- was there a national identity card that applied for everyone in Serbia and Montenegro and were there separate identity cards for those two republics? Do you know what the requirements were?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia had its own Law on Identity Cards, and the Republic of Montenegro had its own. Given the fact that in addition to their student records, our students also are asked to provide IDs at their exams, I've had opportunity to see for myself and I have realised that the two look differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, that's all I had on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say at the moment, Mr. Hannis, I don't understand what the Law on Identity Cards between 1990 and 1999 was, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, then just a couple more questions regarding the decrees. I think you've said it was your understanding there were 16 decrees in all that were issued during the 78 days of war when President Milutinovic was in that position to issue decrees because the National Assembly could not meet during the state of war. These four were -- came through you because they fell under the area of expertise regarding legal matters that you were responsible for, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe the other 12 all seem to have come from your -- one of your fellow deputy prime ministers, Mr. Seselj, who was responsible for the economy, matters related to that. Is that consistent with your understanding? Who were the other three deputy prime ministers in the government in March and April of 1999, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Professor Milovan Bojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, of course, Mr. Seselj. I was to -- I can't remember. I'm already feeling very tired. We did read the relevant portion from the Official Gazette yesterday, didn't we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just have a pause --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit was shown in the court this morning. It is -- it has its number and I don't see why --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I thought the exhibit I saw this morning was -- perhaps I'm mistaken. I saw an earlier one with five deputy prime ministers but Mr. Seselj wasn't one of them, so I assume there was a change at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Both exhibits were -- the Official Gazettes were both the 1994 and the 1998 government members and the vice-presidents was -- was opened -- was exhibited in the court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can give me just one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 1D260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you a tab number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour, I have to find it in -- 1D260. I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm sorry, Your Honour, we cannot locate it. I'm sure that I showed it this morning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got it, Tomislav Nikolic and Dragomir Tomic; Milovan Bojic; myself, Ratko Markovic. Tomislav Nikolic, Dragomir Tomic, and Vojislav Seselj, this is number 7, the red tab. I was involved in the work of two different cabinets. It's very difficult to keep track of all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And with regard to those three others that you named, Mr. Tomic, Mr. Bojic, and Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us what their portfolios were, what areas were they responsible for, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic was in charge of social activities, culture, the health system, anything other than the economy. I think Mr. Nikolic was in charge of public companies, and Mr. Tomic was in charge of commerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think one last area of questions about the four decrees. How -- what was the process before you signed it and passed it on? Was there a discussion in the cabinet or was it merely presented to you to rubber-stamp and pass on? How did that work? How did you decide what was appropriate to rise to the level of being issued as a wartime decree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same thing applied as applied to the work of any collective body. The cabinet had an agenda that was determined ahead of time. Materials were provided in relation to each of the items on the agenda. First there was discussion, and then came decisions. Minutes were taken of each of the cabinet meetings. Once a decision was taken, it would be signed on behalf of the government by a -- by whichever minister was in charge of a particular area. I said several days ago that it was the prime minister who tasked the individual members of the cabinet with their respective responsibilities. The Law on the Government or the Law on Ministries said nothing about the specific areas that members of a cabinet were supposed to be in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said it worked the same as work of any collective body, but who got to vote on particular issues? Did it require unanimous agreement before this would go on or could you make the ultimate decision because you were the prime minister in charge of that particular topic? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision-making process in the cabinet was prescribed by the law and by the rules of procedure governing the work of the cabinet. Decisions were made as a rule by consensus. All of the cabinets that I was involved in were coalition cabinets, which means that what was required was a consensus by all of the partners involved. Each and every cabinet member attending a particular session had the right to involve themselves in the discussion. No cabinet meeting could be held without a minimum of those required present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the quorum was for government meetings?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quorum was the majority of the total number of members of the entire cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry, just so I can be clear. That -- those members of the cabinet would include the prime minister, the five deputy prime ministers, and the ministers of each of the republic ministries, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This also included ministers without portfolio. The number of those was always rather low. There were normally a handful of those, and their responsibilities were defined by the prime minister, whereas all the other ministers had their responsibilities defined by the Law on Ministries. The Law on Ministries provided detail provisions for the work of any of the ministers taking part in the work of the cabinet. Therefore, there were those ministers who headed ministries within a cabinet and those without portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many ministers without portfolio there were in the cabinet in March/April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can have a look at the decision on appointments to the cabinet. This is a decision that we mentioned a while ago. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 7 marked in red.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep confusing red and grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see about the second cabinet that I was involved in, there was seven ministers without portfolio. There were precious few in the first one, I think as many as three, but even that can be checked. Yes, in the first cabinet there were three such ministers, this is at tab 1, there were three ministers without portfolio in the first and seven in the next one. Seven ministers without portfolio and 23 ministers who actually headed specific ministries. Five deputy prime ministers and a prime minister, a total of 36 members. That is how many different members the cabinet comprised in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could both of the witness's microphones please be switched on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you said the ministers without portfolio were hand-picked. Who picked them, the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were picked in the same way as those who headed specific ministries. They were appointed by the parliament, the People's Assembly, at the proposal of the prime minister. But the difference between them on the one hand and those ministers who headed actual ministries was that they didn't have their specific area prescribed by law. They were assigned responsibilities by the prime minister. Sometimes he would give someone, for example, the assignment of monitoring problems related to self-government and sometimes related to a different issue that may or may not have arisen. But their principal relationship was to the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to these four decrees regarding matters related to internal security, identity cards, do you recall the discussions that were had regarding any of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any discussions like that. Maybe I simply wasn't party to any such discussions. Once again I have to underline the fact that the circumstances prevailing in the country were quite irregular. It was difficult to travel across the country. The cabinet secretariat was in a different building altogether and the government meetings took place elsewhere. The ministers were facing a great deal of hardship even trying to reach the building where a session was taking place. The normal communication between cabinet members at the time was disrupted due to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you for that. Let me move on now. I want to ask you some questions about your expert report. You mentioned a little bit ago, Professor, that you were tired. Do you feel okay to continue? Do you want a break?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, thank you. I prefer to continue. There's no reason to stall the work of this court. My age is my own problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a similar problem, Professor. Your expert report - I don't know what tab that is in your binder - number 1 in your grey binder I guess, in the introduction the very first sentence - and this is Exhibit 1D682 for the record - it says: "The institution of the president of the republic was the most contentious issue in political and expert discussions at the time of and immediately after the adoption of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1990." And you note that: "At this time the Republic of Serbia for the first time obtained an executive head of state." Now, are you referring to the president as an executive head of state, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But as I understand your testimony earlier this week, he was not an operational executive?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of his powers, he was no different from a president of the republic under those constitutional systems where a president of the republic is appointed or elected by the parliament. He has no effective powers, such as is normally the case, in textbook parliamentary republics such as Italy and Germany, where presidents do not have any great powers. The same thing applied to the president of the republic in the Republic of Serbia. Although he's directly elected by the citizens and directly revoked or recalled by the citizens, he has the -- he enjoys the greatest extent of democratic responsibility. But the president's powers did not rise to quite the same level and that's why theorists do not see Serbia at the same level as countries with a semi-presidential system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance to my learned friend. I believe he has been misled by not appropriate translation and it was raised by Your Honours the very first day. The word in Serbian is "inokosan" and we tried to find the proper explanation. It is not executive, it is "inokosan" an individual or -- it was translated "sole" or head of state or something like that. If you remember, it was the issue we have been talking about the very first day. Inokosan, we said individual or -- "executive" is definitely a wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it can be clarified, Professor, by you telling us what was the difference between the role of the president prior to 1990 and the role of the president from 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the 1974 constitution, Serbia had no president of the republic. It did have a Presidency, though, which was a collegial body. It had some members and had the following function. It had the function of the head of state of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
