utterances.text: I think that that is an adequate answer to the issue that arises here because the detail of that's immaterial. It's important to concentrate on the detailed powers of the president from 1990 onwards. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in describing the controversy or the debate that took place around the time the constitution came into being regarding the office of the president, you said that some of the critics of the constitution claimed that the powers of the president under this new constitution were unusually broad, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those same critics read it as making the president the most powerful constitutional institution in Serbia. Isn't that what some of those people said?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia was adopted in 1990, the multi-party system of the Republic of Serbia was just in its initial stage. And at that time the constitution of 1990 focused on the constitution of the president of the republic, and that is what most criticism was voiced at. And it was being said that it was being tailor-made for the then president to the Presidency, Slobodan Milosevic. And that is precisely why this criticism was more of a form of inter-party political strife in Serbia rather than being argumented in an objective sense, impartial sense based on scholarly arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us who some of the critics were, the critics were, I take it, academics, law professors, intelligent people with some understanding of the law and constitutions, right? We're not talking about the general public making these kind of criticisms, are we?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I mentioned that in my expert opinion. I mentioned their words, the text that they actually uttered on that occasion. So it was some of the scholars who spoke up for the same reasons, political reasons, while putting into the background scholarly criteria. They criticised the institution of the president of the republic. The best answer to the question as to what the true reaches of the office of the president are was given by Mr. Djindjic in 1997 when he said - and we quoted that here - that that office does not have any particular responsibilities, that the president of the republic cannot even appoint a prime minister designate of his own free will and he cannot of his own accord dissolve the Assembly, that it's only a symbolical office. At that time, Mr. Djindjic was one of the opposition leaders and this is his very own statement, and he said that he himself would not run for that particular office. So as soon as President Milosevic ceased to hold the office of the president of the republic, automatically all criticism of that office ceased. And what I said in my expert opinion is that it was only authors of textbooks in constitutional law and professors of law at universities that dealt with these questions. The broad public became totally disinterested in the office of the president of the republic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess I'm struggling with this controversy because, I don't know, it seems to me if you're looking at a document to analyse the document, it says what it says and your opinion about what it means, for example, about the relative powers of the president vis-a-vis the National Assembly and/or the government, that shouldn't change depending on who the president is. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree. At that time as well the president had the same powers that President Boris Tadic had according to this constitution, that is the president in office right now. So the powers are completely the same. However, the personality of Slobodan Milosevic had this magnetism. So critics focused on that particular office in order to go for a political show-down with him. That is what criticism of the office of the president of the republic was based on. He did not have any greater powers than the presidents who came after him. However, as a person, as a personality, he had this charisma. And therefore, critics of the 1990 constitution focused on the office of the president of the republic because he held that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Professor, as a lawyer and as a constitutional law scholar and someone whose written constitutions, would you agree with me that one of the things that drafters of constitutions often try to do is trying to strike a balance between having -- I don't know, having a document with 1.000 articles with every possible contingency outlined in strict rules and having a very rigid inflexible document which has certain advantages because everything's clear and everyone knows where the lines are; and on the other hand, having a very flexible document with a lot of ambiguity in it to allow for changes to circumstances in the future and not having the necessity to amend the constitution every six weeks or six months because of new changes. Isn't that part of the challenge in creating a constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, it is a challenge. The authors of the constitution, or rather, all authors of constitutions have to bear in mind a balance between these two extremes. That is to say, to what extent one should go into detail and in this way make the constitution short-lived, or should one opt for a constitution containing principles only and thus making it longer lived. One of the reasons why the American constitution is still valid for over 200 years is precisely because that is what its authors opted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And almost every constitution is going to have some ambiguity built into it. It's just the nature of language and the nature of lawyers as wordsmiths for that to happen, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. I agree with you. Answers to these ambiguities are given by constitutional practice, by jurisprudence, or interpretations provided by the Constitutional Court in its rulings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at least the experience that I'm familiar with in the United States is that partly because of that ambiguity in a constitution, the office of the president can be seen as being stronger or not so strong depending in part on the individual who's holding office, because of how they work with the ambiguities inherent in our constitution. Would you agree that's how it works in real life with presidents and constitutions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree, and that is why in America there are some great presidents, as it is said, although they all had the same powers in accordance with the constitution of 1777, but some of them were simply strong personalities and therefore, gave an imprint through their presidency. On the other hand, there were presidents who went by unnoticed on terms of their influence, except for the fact that they held the office of president in a given period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And because of that factor, isn't that the reason that some of the critics raised such an alarm at the time was because Mr. Milosevic, a strong personality, was in that position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, that was the reason. He was a person with a great deal of charisma and who was a party leader. So a president of the republic who does not have a strong political party behind him is handicapped, one who is not a leader of a major political party. He cannot have the same kind of aura that a president who's a party leader can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. One other thing in your introduction in your expert report when you described the controversy, you say: "Those who argued that the new constitution did not provide for a strong president but only one who had somewhat broader powers than a monarch in a constitutional parliamentary monarchy." And can you give us an example of a constitutional parliamentary monarchy. Would that be Queen Elizabeth in England?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we look at the powers of the president of the republic according to the constitution of 1990 along with the explanations we've already provided, he simply cannot apply some of these powers because the federal constitution reserves that for the federal state. Part of them cannot be carried out because certain laws had not been passed on the basis of which he could exercise these powers. So when these powers were measured against the Queen of England, well they're about the same because the Queen of England cannot decide herself who the prime minister designate is going to be, nor can she dissolve parliament, nor can she refuse to support a law that was passed in parliament. I remember the last person who did that was Queen Ann as far back as 1707, the last British monarch to have done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, regarding the powers of the president under Article 83 of that constitution, the last one, item number 12, which is something I refer to as sort of the catch-all provision that says: "The president can conduct other affairs in accordance with the constitution." There are similar sort of catch-all powers for each the government and the National Assembly in that constitution, correct, not worded exactly the same but generically similar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant here are the powers of the president that are not concentrated, not exactly enumerated in Article 83, but rather stipulated in other articles, specifically 84, 85, 89, and 132, paragraph 1. Nowhere else does the constitution give any powers to the president. This provision means that a law cannot give him any new powers, and we saw what happened with the law that gave such authority the president at one point when the Constitutional Court ruled on this, the law ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have a question about that. You say that it means -- "in accordance with the constitution" means in accordance with his presidential powers under the articles in, I think, 84 through 89 or 84, 85, and 89, and 132. But if that were the case, why wouldn't item number 12 just simply say: "And conduct other affairs in accordance with Articles 84, 85, 89, and 132"? Then there would be no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. It can be put that way, too. It's a matter of expression, legal technique, if you will. It is more concise if it is put the way you proposed just now. But it can also be put this way, too. Now, the question is one of affinity, the affinity of the person drafting the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were part of the constitutional commission that drafted the constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many people were on that commission?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That constitutional commission -- well, it's a big body. It had tens of members, but a smaller body was created out of it called the coordination committee of the commission and that body had 10 or 12 members. They established the draft constitution which was afterwards adopted by the constitutional commission and then presented to the Assembly for its further discussion in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you talk with us a bit about how that worked. The coordinating committee, were you a member of the coordinating committee?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was a member of the coordinating commission. The president of the coordination commission was Mr. Slobodan Vucetic. He was also the last president of the Constitutional Court of Serbia, and the commission was formulate -- was actually a working team of experts; and quite literally, they wrote the text. Since I was a person who dealt directly with constitutional law for years, I was asked to come up with a structure of the constitution, whereas we together sought specific solutions at committee meetings, or rather, meetings of the coordinating commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the -- was there a single overall head of the entire commission?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was. Ex officio it was the president of the National Assembly; at that time, it was Mr. Zoran Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he do any of the actual work of drafting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not do any of the actual work for a simple reason. He had a degree in agriculture, so he was not an expert in law. So -- well, on that team, on the coordinating commission, there were people who had professional knowledge of writing regulations and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the role of the coordinating commission vis-a-vis the entire commission? Was the coordinating commission the one that was doing the actual hands-on drafting or doing the editing and proofing of drafting that came from the wider commission? What was your role?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our role was to prepare texts for the constitutional commission. So this was a working team. I remember that these meetings of ours went on until late at night, until dawn almost. It is true that the constitution is short, it has only 136 articles, but all of that had to be formulated. It was necessary to debate different solutions before that and to reach agreement. So this team did most of the work concerning the constitution. As for the constitutional commission, perhaps there would just be proposals for redrafting some of the provisions, but there weren't any proposals that would change the very substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I have just a question with your permission. Now, did you have before you certain norms to be kept there for framing of the constitution and also any grundnorm, and how did you include political thoughts according to these norms in the constitution? Who guided all that and what were those norms, if you could briefly tell us. Thank you, learned Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, we proceeded from the historical point in time that Serbia was in. An attempt was made to do away with the socialist self-management system that had existed until then. We believed that the constitution that was closest to the situation that Serbia was facing then, of course, it would have to be modified in terms of political culture, history, Serbia's constitutional history, because Serbia does have a rich constitutional history. It passed its first constitution as far back as 1835. It was our belief that this was the 1958 constitution of the 5th French Republic. So as far as the organisation of power is concerned, the main ideas came from the French constitution of 1958. As for heading the work of the team, I said a few minutes ago that the chairman of the coordinating commission was Mr. Slobodan Vucetic. He chaired the meetings and the members of the coordinating commission very actively participated in the work of the commission. So it was team work. The constitution was a team effort. Journalists and other writers simplified matters and kept referring to me as the writer or the author of the constitution, which is impossible. A single person cannot be the author of a constitution, that is impossible. Several people have to be involved in writing a constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But did you, sir, have representation from the various ethnic groups which constituted the populace and were they heard and what were the political thoughts expressed and how were they accommodated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. This constitutional commission was a commission from the old period, so to speak, when there was socialist self-management in Yugoslavia, where great attention was paid to the equality of nations, of ethnic rights, of the Yugoslav nations and nationalities, ethnic minorities. At that time, all bodies were constituted on the basis of equal representation, parity. In every body there were representatives of different ethnic communities and of different national minorities. On the constitutional commission as well we had such persons. I cannot remember exactly now, it was a long time ago, but I do remember, for example, that there was an Albanian Mr. Tefki Lugixhi [phoen], that he was one of the members. There were other Albanians who were members of the constitutional commission too. Of course, it depended on their professional knowledge and on their political wishes that were clearly defined. And then they took part in these debates accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And did you decide the issues on a majority vote within the commission or not when an issue was discussed? Thank you. And that was the last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the constitutional commission we always decided by majority vote, but the chairman, Mr. Sokolovic, always tried to reach a consensus to have general agreement, not to have any out-voting. Efforts were made to satisfy all to a maximum and to find a compromise. You will see that in this constitution an archaic term was kept which doesn't really meaning anything linguistically, the term "narodnost". The term "narodnost" was a term used for national minorities because representatives of national minorities believed that the word "minority" was offensive to them, so this term remained. And all foreigners wondered when they heard the translation into foreign languages what this "narodnost" meant and it's basically the same thing as a national minority, however, respecting the feelings of the members of national minorities that term was kept. Then already in the preamble, for instance, the preamble of that constitution you see proceeding from, et cetera, et cetera, the centuries-long struggle, and then it says historical development and joint life of all the peoples and nationalities in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you said that typically I think the votes were taken by majority, the chairman tried to have a consensus reached. But I take it that sometimes that didn't happen, that they couldn't have a consensus on portions of this constitution. So who was the final arbiter in those situations, was it just simply if there was a majority in favour it went in or did the chairman have the authority to say yes or no to a controversial provision? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was decided by majority vote at the time. I can't remember exactly which chapters of the constitution were involved, but I remember, for example, the article declaring the equality of various types of ownership where one of the possible kinds of property is listed as social property, this is Article 56. They wanted this term, socially-owned property to be erased, so that the only ones remaining would be state, private, and co-op types of ownership. Some members of the commission believed that socially-owned property had to be erased, and I remember who wanted that to be erased. For example, Professor Budimir Kosutic who was a member of the constitutional commission. However, by voting we decided that socially-owned property ought to remain because it was a reality at the time. We also believed that the market was that criteria which would decide which types of ownership would remain and which wouldn't. In the new constitution, we no longer have this term "socially-owned property."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it did. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the first third. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, of the 136 articles, were there any of those that you were opposed to that got put in the constitution in spite of your personal disagreement or objection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, for example, disagreed with the term "narodnost," which means ethnic minority. I also was against the formulation where member of parliament represents the citizens of the territory from which he was elected. This is in Article 86. However, the mentality from the old system was still quite strong. So an absolutely free mandate was something that could not be accepted. Therefore, they believed that a member of the parliament had to be linked to the electorate that elected him. Perhaps I was against some other formulations as well that found their way into the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to Article 83, number 12, under the powers of the president and what I call the catch-all phrase about: "Conduct other affairs in accordance with the constitution." I had proposed an alternative way of phrasing. Would you agree there's one way it could be done, but you said this one was the one that was preferred. Would you agree with me, however, Professor, under this one there is some room for an argument to be made that there's an ambiguity here upon which a strong president could argue that: Well, I take that as meaning I can do anything that's consistent with the constitution and for which there is no specific prohibition against my engaging in that activity. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I think that that would not be possible. He can only exercise the power explicitly given to him by the constitution, not the power that he supposes he has within the spirit of the constitution and his constitutional position, because his responsibility in relation to this constitution is based on a violation of the constitution. He can only be recalled if the Assembly establishes that he violated the constitution, and he definitely violated the constitution if he exercised the power not granted to him by the constitution. All powers need to be explicitly specified. There are no assumed powers. So you cannot give it this interpretation that the president of the republic believes to have some power. For example, the power to initiate legislative procedure. No. The constitution quite clearly spells out who has the legislative initiative, and the president does not have it. He has no right to address directly the parliament, members of the parliament, and so on. This paragraph in Article 83 means that in addition to these powers, he has only those that are explicitly spelled out by the constitution, not some powers that he assumes he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm recalling your testimony earlier in the week when we were talking about the promotion of General Lukic, and that seemed to be something where the president presumed he had a power that seemed to be in the constitution until the Constitutional Court said otherwise, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. It is not that he believed that, rather the Law on the Ranks of the Members of the Ministry of the Interior gave him that power and the Law on Ranks of the Members of the Ministry of the Interior in Articles 6 and 10 gave such a power to the president of the republic. And the president of the republic applied or exercised that power all the way up until the Constitutional Court said that the president of the republic is not entitled to that power because that is not in accordance with the constitution. And the constitution referred to the very same reason that we mentioned now; namely, that the president of the republic can have only those powers which you can see is in the decision of the Constitutional Court here, that the president of the republic can have only those powers which are explicitly stated in the constitution. This is why the law in its provisions granting to the president the powers not recognised by the constitution was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'll come back to a related topic later. In your testimony on Monday, I think this was at page 12877 of the transcript, you were talking about the situation in 1990 when the new constitution was passed and that there was a danger of secession of certain republics. And you mentioned that the Constitution of Serbia provided sort of in anticipation of a possible constitutional vacuum, it provided attributes of an independent state to Serbia. Can you explain to us what attributes of an independent state are or the ones that were provided for in the constitution. Is that the army and conducting foreign affairs? Are those the matters you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the matters that I was referring to. A federal unit cannot have its autonomous foreign policy in any federation in the world; nor can it have its own Ministry of Foreign Affairs; nor can it be represented in international organisations, such as the UN, for example; nor can it have its own army. So these are the reserve powers reserved for the president of the republic, and some others listed in Article 72 of the constitution which specified the competencies of Serbia. See, this Article 72 is completely atypical, and it exists precisely because of the situation in which Serbia was at the time. In case of secession, they didn't want there to be any competencies for which nobody was in charge. And this is why these competencies were listed in Article 72, even though some of them fell within the jurisdiction of the Federation. This Constitution of Serbia in Article 135 clearly says that everything that falls within the jurisdiction of the Federation, but also within the jurisdiction of Serbia, will be carried out in accordance with the Constitution of the Federation. The supremacy is given here to the Constitution of the Federation, which is quite normal anywhere in the world. Due to this atypical situation in which Serbia found itself in 1990, the Constitution of Serbia contains such provisions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'll have some questions about Article 135 later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You made reference to Serbia as being a federal unit. I take it you mean the Republic of Serbia was a federal unit within the Federation of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the autonomous provinces federal units as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not. Autonomous provinces are not federal units. One can see that in Article 2 of the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974. In that article - and that article reads that Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia comprises six federal units and it clearly specifies which ones, without listing two autonomous provinces. Autonomous provinces were within the composition of Serbia as a federal unit. So in Article 2 of the 1974 constitution, the structure of the then-Yugoslav Federation was established, and according to that article the federation had six federal units. One of those six had within its composition two autonomous provinces. We have the text of the 1974 constitution somewhere here, and if you wish I can read it from my own copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's stop here for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before stopping, can you remind me, Professor, whether an amendment to the 1990 constitution would require a referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you wished to amend that constitution, roughly how long would it take for the process to be undertaken and completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taken into account the deadlines in the Law on Referendum, time-limits in that law, and in order, or rather, if the Assembly was as expeditious as possible, it would take at least two months, because the draft amendments had to be adopted in the National Assembly by two-thirds majority. And then at a referendum by majority votes of voters in registry lists, that had to be adopted too. And from the moment the referendum was scheduled until it was held, there needed a certain time-limit to lapse, as was established by the law, and I think that it would take at least two months for that to be done according to the 1990 constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that completes our sitting for today. Your cross-examination will continue tomorrow at 9.00. Meanwhile, can you leave the courtroom again with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the court is adjourned until 9.00 tomorrow.
